title: Three friendships
hook: Aristotle: friendships of use, of pleasure, and of goodness (Nicomachean Ethics 8.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aristophanes and the round people. Your line was the half. Did you thank someone who completes you? Today, from the dinner party to a lecture room, and a word from earlier this week: philia. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

A crowded group chat. Some people are in it because you work together. Some are in it because you have fun together. And maybe one or two are in it because, if everything else fell away, you'd still want them in your life. Aristotle noticed the same sorting long before phones, in his Nicomachean Ethics, and he gave it a shape. Today, his three kinds of friendship, and the slow one at the end.

First, friends of use. Some friendships rest on what each person gets: a coworker, a neighbor who lends tools. Aristotle doesn't sneer at these. But when the usefulness ends, he says, the friendship tends to end too. Second, friends of pleasure. Some rest on enjoyment: people who are fun, who make you laugh. He notices these among the young, who change what they enjoy, and so make and lose friends quickly. Third, friends of the good. The complete kind, Aristotle says, is between people who are good and alike in goodness, who wish good to each other for the other's own sake. These friendships turn out pleasant and useful too, but that isn't why they exist, and they last as long as the people stay good. Fourth, salt eaten together. Such friendships are rare, he says, and slow. As the old saying goes, people can't know each other until they've eaten salt together. The wish for friendship comes fast; the friendship itself takes time. Philia is Aristotle's word for all three kinds. He doesn't call friends of use fake friends. He calls them a smaller kind, and he keeps the larger kind for people who want each other's good.
screen: `FRIENDS OF USE.` · `FRIENDS OF PLEASURE.` · `FRIENDS OF THE GOOD.` · `SALT EATEN TOGETHER.` · then, large: `PHILIA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let a few friends' faces come to mind, without ranking them. Notice gently which friendships rest on use, which on enjoyment, and whether one rests on something more: on wanting each other's good. There's no need to judge any of them. If one name stands out, stay with it. Remember the time it took, the meals and the hard days, the salt eaten together. If no name comes, that's an honest answer too, and a friendship like that can still begin. The bell holds the time.
Philia. The Greek word for the love between friends. Aristotle used it for all three kinds: friends of use, of pleasure, and of the good. Today's word.
Your line: friends of the good. Today, name one friend of the good, to yourself or to them, and do one small thing purely for their sake. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship, from books eight and nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, are studied in philosophy and ethics courses, and some readers use them to reflect on their own friendships.

notes: Aristotle paraphrased throughout (no translation on the validator's public-domain list).

8.3: friendships of utility (associated with the old) and pleasure (with the young) are easily dissolved; the complete friendship of good people alike in virtue is rare, requires time, and the proverb about eating salt together. The script mentions only the young; confirm framing.
'Philia is Aristotle's word for all three kinds' — he does call utility and pleasure friendships philia 'by resemblance' (8.4); confirm 'a smaller kind' is fair.
Word 'philia' was also glossed on day 819; this day goes deeper into Aristotle's use.
Audit: no changes. Use and pleasure dissolving, the young, complete friendship rare and slow, the salt proverb, and 'the wish comes fast, the friendship takes time' all match 8.3.
